title: Banned from Harvard
hook: the Divinity School Address so upset the clergy that, the usual account goes, Harvard didn't ask him back for a long time

segments.voice: Yesterday, the snowstorm behind the preacher: the real snow outside the window saying more than the sermon inside. Your line was the snow was real. Did you catch yourself repeating something you'd only heard? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-three.

A guest is invited to speak to a class of young men about to become ministers. The guest is polite, soft-spoken, a former minister himself. And in long, beautiful sentences he tells the room that the churches these graduates are about to serve have lost touch with the living soul. Then he goes home. The reaction does not stay in the room. It goes into print, sharply. And by the usual account, Harvard does not ask Ralph Waldo Emerson back to speak for a long, long time. Today is about what happens when you say the hard thing.
screen: `A POLITE GUEST.` → `A HARD MESSAGE.` → `NOT ASKED BACK.`

segments.voice: First, what he said. Yesterday's snowstorm was one part of this same talk. The deeper part was Emerson's charge that the churches had made too much of the person of Jesus, and too little of the divine life Jesus pointed to in every soul. And he gave the young ministers this advice, in his own words: "go alone; to refuse the good models, even those which are sacred in the imagination of men, and dare to love God without mediator or veil." Second, why it hurt. For the ministers and professors in that room, Jesus was not a model to set aside. He was the center of the faith, the one through whom God is known. To them, Emerson seemed to be pulling the floor out. Their alarm was sincere, and it came from what they loved. A scholar who had taught at the school answered in print, calling it a new form of unbelief. Third, what Emerson did next. Almost nothing. He didn't publish a reply. When a friend and colleague wrote asking him to defend his views, Emerson answered that he couldn't give arguments for them. He could only say what he saw. Fourth, the lesson anyone can take, whichever side of that room they'd have sat on. Saying a true thing, as you see it, can cost you. It can cost you an invitation, or a friendship. Emerson stayed gentle in manner while saying something hard in substance. True and kind don't always arrive together. But you can try to keep them in the same sentence.
screen: `MADE TOO MUCH OF THE PERSON.` · `TO THEM, THE CENTER OF THE FAITH.` · `NO ARGUMENTS, ONLY WHAT HE SAW.` · `HARD SUBSTANCE, GENTLE MANNER.` · then, large: `TRUE AND KIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one true thing to say kindly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you've been holding something back from. A worry about them. A disagreement. A piece of honest feedback. Don't rehearse a speech. Just find the true thing, in as few words as you can. Then look at the person in your mind, and ask how you'd say it if you wanted them to hear it, not just to have said it. Let the words soften without going false. Hold the true thing and the kindness together. The bell holds the time.
Banned from Harvard. The usual account of what Emerson's Divinity School Address cost him: a sincere uproar, a sharp reply in print, and a long time before he was asked back. Today's word.
Your line: true and kind. Today, say the one true thing you found, to the person it's for, and say it as gently as it can be said. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Emerson's Divinity School Address is often read as a case study in speaking an unpopular conviction: what he said, how sincerely his hearers objected, and how he declined to argue back.

notes: Confirm exact wording of the quotation: 'Let me admonish you, first of all, to go alone; to refuse the good models, even those which are sacred in the imagination of men, and dare to love God without mediator or veil.' The script quotes from 'go alone'.

The outline hook says Harvard didn't invite him back 'for decades'; the script says only 'by the usual account ... for a long time' and gives no number of years. A scholar should confirm the length and wording.

The professor who answered in print is Andrews Norton; his reply's title is commonly given as 'The Latest Form of Infidelity'. The script does not name him or quote the title; it says 'a new form of unbelief'. Confirm.
The letter to Henry Ware Jr. is paraphrased (he could not give arguments; he did not know what arguments mean in reference to the expression of a thought). Confirm.
The hook's 'small audience' is dramatization, not sourced; cut if a reviewer prefers.
The Christian objection is framed fairly and the script does not side with Emerson or his critics; a Christian reviewer should check the line 'the one through whom God is known'.

Editor: cut the unsourced 'small audience' detail and 'graduation' framing; Andrews Norton had already left his professorship, so 'one of the senior professors' became 'a scholar who had taught at the school'; match pair and myth adjusted.
